sources.note: Shows that a perturbation-based selection rule's apparent 31.8-point gain over majority voting in vision-language test-time scaling is a decoding-format effect, by adding a control that spends the same short-answer budget on the unperturbed image and finds it matches or beats the perturbation rule everywhere.
sources.title: It's the Decoding Format, Not the Perturbation: Auditing Consistency-Based Selection for Vision-Language Test-Time Scaling

sources.note: Diagnoses label-free RLVR's collapse as a shortcut in which the same answer-level consensus signal both estimates the reward and receives the gradient, and fixes it by masking the answer span from updates entirely — so a reward can only be raised by improving the reasoning that produces the answer.
sources.title: Don't Peek at the Answer: Outcome-Masked Group Relative Policy Optimization for Label-Free RLVR

sources.note: Allocates test-time samples per prompt with a fuzzy controller over human-readable difficulty and confidence signals, and — under a selector-matched protocol that isolates the budget policy from the answer selector — reports the result honestly as an accuracy-compute tradeoff rather than an accuracy gain.
sources.title: Interpretable Adaptive Sampling for LLM Test-Time Scaling

sources.note: Spends test-time compute on iteratively refining each sampled rollout rather than on drawing more of them, then majority-votes the refined answers, with no verifier.
sources.title: Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning

sources.note: Removes external supervision from on-policy self-distillation by building a pseudo-solution from the model's own majority vote and using it as privileged teacher context rather than as a scalar reward, then distilling only on the completions that disagree with it.
sources.title: On-Policy Self-Distillation without Any Supervision

sources.note: Treats test-time scaling as routing rather than budgeting -- cheap evidence decides whether a decision is already settled, and expensive verification is spent only on candidates that can still change the answer -- and evaluates every baseline by replaying it over the same stored candidate pool so that only the allocation decision differs.
sources.title: CoBa: Cost-Effective Test-Time Scaling via Compute-Balanced Routing

sources.note: Shows on four internal Netflix verification tasks that explicit reasoning usually degrades subjective judgement, that applying RLVR to fix it makes the policy abandon deliberation for short heuristic guessing, and that a length bonus gated on answer correctness is what stops the collapse.
sources.title: LLM Reasoning for Subjective Tasks: Failure Modes, Mitigation, and Dynamic Reasoning Routing

sources.note: Asks whether a fixed inference budget buys more accuracy spent on varying the input than on varying the reasoning path, and finds paraphrase aggregation beats self-consistency on five of six benchmarks at matched compute.
sources.title: Test-Time Augmentation for LLMs: When Input Diversity Beats Output Diversity at Matched Compute

sources.note: Asks whether a candidate pool contains enough signal to select from itself, by compiling sampled CAD programs into 3D models and returning the one that agrees most with the rest -- and finds this verifier-free rule beats a vision-language verifier on every geometric metric when both select from the identical pool.
sources.title: Test-Time Scaling for CAD Generation via Verifier-Free Consensus Selection

sources.note: Shows that selecting the most confident rollout can be worse than picking at random, because uniformly high confidence signals a failure to explore rather than a well-supported answer, and replaces maximisation with a temporal criterion that penalises early certainty while requiring late certainty.
sources.title: Consilience for Verifier-Free Test-Time Scaling

sources.note: Measures, under a pre-registered confirmatory design, how often majority-vote self-consistency lowers per-problem accuracy on a hard science benchmark, and shows that two cheap verifier-free gates recover essentially none of the headroom a per-problem oracle marks out.
sources.title: When Self-Consistency Backfires: Majority Vote Hurts the Majority of Hard Science Problems for Small LLMs

sources.note: Reallocates half of a test-time sampling budget from generating more solutions to asking the same model to refute a handful of decision-critical claims extracted from each trace, then weights the consensus vote by how many claims survive.
sources.title: Claim-Level Reliability Assessment for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning

sources.note: Verifies correctness without training by comparing a reasoning trace's start-to-end hidden-state delta against two class centroids built from labelled experience.
sources.title: Your Reasoning Model is Secretly a Reward Model - Optimization-Free Verification from Experience

sources.note: Stops self-consistency sampling by Bayesian posterior over which answer is the mode, and proves that tracking only the top two answer counts plus an aggregate is enough for asymptotic optimality.
sources.title: Optimal Bayesian Stopping for Efficient Inference of Consistent LLM Answers

sources.note: Trains reasoning models to be concise in proportion to difficulty by modulating the token penalty and the target length per problem, and fixes a distortion that naive reward weighting introduces into group-normalized RL.
sources.title: The Overthinker's DIET: Cutting Token Calories with DIfficulty-AwarE Training

sources.note: Proves that parameterizing an outcome reward as the log-likelihood ratio between a policy and a reference model makes the per-step Q value fall out of the same model for free, so a process reward model can be obtained by training an outcome reward model on response-level labels alone.
sources.title: Free Process Rewards without Process Labels

sources.note: Gives two aggregation algorithms whose failure probability provably decays to zero as inference compute grows, assuming only that the model can sometimes be right and can compare two solutions better than chance.
sources.title: Provable Scaling Laws for the Test-Time Compute of Large Language Models

sources.note: Introduces EDIS, a trajectory-level score that measures how unstably token entropy evolves during generation, and uses it to select better reasoning rollouts at inference and to curate training samples in RL.
sources.title: EDIS: Diagnosing LLM Reasoning via Entropy Dynamics

instructions:
Write the wiki definition for 'majority voting'.

The sources below are every archived paper and talk that mentions it. Define it as they use it: if they disagree, say so; if the term is used loosely, say that too.

`related` is the one part of the note nothing can work out on its own. The wiki already links entities that turn up in the same summary; what it cannot see is the neighbour a reader would actually want next — the generation before this one, the benchmark it was built to beat, the method it replaces. Name those. Leave the list empty rather than repeating what the sources already put side by side.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

aliases: string - other names the sources use for the same thing
output_schema.definition: string - two to four sentences defining the entity as the cited sources use it, not as a textbook would
output_schema.kind: string - one of: concept, method, dataset, model
related: string - name of a neighbouring entity worth linking to. Kept as you give it and never derived away, so name what a reader should turn to next rather than what happens to appear alongside this. Answering again replaces the whole list; an empty list retracts

result.definition: Returning the answer most sampled responses agree on, and across 18 sources the aggregation baseline everything is measured against and almost everything beats. Its failure has a theoretical statement and an empirical one. Theoretically it converges to zero whenever some incorrect answer is individually more probable than the correct one, so more samples make it worse rather than better in that regime. Empirically that regime is reachable: on a hard graduate science benchmark it lowers per-problem accuracy on 56.6 and 65.7 percent of problems for two models while barely moving the aggregate, and in one test-time-training setting it actively lowers average accuracy (36.92 to 35.09) by converging toward an incorrect consensus. It is also beaten by every reweighting scheme the archive holds, typically by margins that grow with the sample count -- 60.6 percent against its 46.2 at sixteen samples in one comparison, and 51.7 and 50.9 for two confidence-based selectors in the same table. Used as a training signal rather than a selector, its characteristic damage is localised: one source's KL decomposition shows divergence on answer tokens rising sharply under it while reasoning-token divergence grows slowly, and masking the answer span keeps the former low and stable. The archive's summary position is that it is the right null and the wrong method: it assumes agreement tracks correctness, and the calibration measurements show that on hard problems it does not.
